impertinent

/im-PER-tuh-nent/ — stress on PER · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Someone who is impertinent is rude or disrespectful, especially by speaking or acting toward someone senior as if they were an equal or inferior.

Asking the bride how much the wedding cost was an impertinent question.

Worked Example

During the board meeting, the new intern interrupted the CEO mid-sentence and said, 'That's not how we should do this.' His tone was impertinent.

Im (not) + pertinent (appropriate, fitting). The intern's interruption and manner were not appropriate—he treated a senior executive as an equal rather than with the respect the position demands. Impertinent captures both rudeness and the violation of social hierarchy.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

cheeky: Cheeky means playfully bold past the polite line — mischief delivered with a grin that expects a laugh. Impertinent is the colder offense: real disrespect toward someone senior, with no humor to soften it. A cheeky reply winks at the teacher; an impertinent one challenges her right to be obeyed.

presumptuous: Presumptuous means overstepping what your position allows — helping yourself to a decision, a liberty, or an authority that was never given to you. Impertinent needs rudeness aimed at someone senior; presumptuous needs no rudeness at all, only the quiet assumption that the rules of rank do not apply to you.

flippant: Flippant means treating a serious moment with jokey, offhand unseriousness — wisecracking during a fire drill. Impertinent aims the disrespect at a person, especially someone senior, rather than at an occasion. A flippant remark can offend a whole room without targeting anyone; an impertinent one needs a superior to slight.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

pertinent: the word's literal root, im- + pertinent — not a natural modern antonym, since impertinent's meaning drifted from ‘irrelevant’ to ‘rude’ over the centuries

polite: well-mannered and considerate of others — the modern antonym

Where it sits · how much it disrespects authority — blunt → forward → rude → impertinent

blunt vs. impertinent: A blunt question is honest but tactless, while an impertinent question crosses the line into disrespect.

forward vs. impertinent: A forward comment is a little too bold; an impertinent comment presumes a familiarity it has no right to.

rude vs. impertinent: A rude interruption breaks good manners, but an impertinent interruption disrespects someone's position or authority outright.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — im-

Prefix — im-: not (the form in- takes before b, m, or p) (Latin)

Root — pertinent

Root — pertinent: appropriate, to the point (from Latin pertinere, 'to relate to, concern') (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Im- (not) + pertinent (appropriate, to the point) originally meant just that: 'not appropriate, off the point.' Over the centuries the meaning drifted and narrowed — from irrelevant, to inappropriate, to today's specific sense of rude and disrespectful, especially by speaking out of turn.

Use the root in a new word: pertain

Use the root in a new word: pertain: The lawyer asked only questions that pertain to the case, ignoring everything else.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal

Reach for impertinent when someone is being rude or disrespectful, especially to a social superior or in a formal setting. The word implies not just rudeness but a violation of social protocol and hierarchy. Don't assume the prefix simply means 'not relevant'—the base word's meaning has drifted over centuries.
